# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## Rethinking What a Successful Meeting Looks Like

There is a widespread assumption, rarely stated but deeply felt, that a good meeting is one where everyone walks out nodding. We celebrate alignment. We praise teams that "get on the same page." A meeting that ends in harmony feels productive; a meeting that ends in argument feels like a failure, or at least an unfinished piece of business.

But this intuition deserves scrutiny. Agreement, it turns out, is not always a sign that understanding has been reached. Sometimes it is a sign that understanding has been avoided. People nod for many reasons: because they are tired, because they fear the boss, because the discussion has gone on too long, because they haven't thought carefully yet, or because the plan being proposed is vague enough that everyone can project their own hopes onto it. Genuine agreement—the kind where everyone shares the same picture of what will happen and why—can only be verified when people are willing to say what they actually think. And what they actually think, in the early stages of any hard problem, is often that they disagree.
